newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian aluminium plant in new turmoil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian aluminium plant in new turmoil.

text.p: Russia's Krasnoyarsk aluminium smelter sacked its Western-style director on Tuesday after only two weeks in the job in the latest round of a management upheaval.

Krasnoyarsk, in Siberia, is the world's second biggest aluminium smelter and is a force on the international markets. But boardroom struggles there typify the rough and tumble style of the Russian metals sector.
A news release said the board dropped Igor Vishnyevsky, who is also employed by Swiss-based commodities house Glencore AG, as general director after appointing him earlier this month.
Glencore owns five percent of the smelter.

"We had a good chance when I was general manager to improve the situation at the plant," Vishnyevsky said in Moscow. "My nomination as general manager was quite positively viewed in the Western world..."
The man who replaced him, Gennady Druzhinin, a long-time Krasnoyarsk manager, said Vishnyevsky went because he had not spent enough time in Krasnoyarsk.

"Considering Vishnyevsky has been moving in who knows which direction over the past two weeks, we could no longer tolerate leaving the company without a commander," Druzhinin said by telephone from Krasnoyarsk, in southern Siberia.

The Krasnoyarsk smelter, also known as KrAZ, produced 780,000 tonnes of primary aluminium last year, or 28 percent of total output in Russia, which was the world's largest aluminium exporter and second biggest producer in 1996.
"I doubt it (the change) will affect production," Vishnyevsky said. "The production centres are working well, without any problems."
Krasnoyarsk is no stranger to the headlines. In 1994 it crossed British metals company Trans-World Group off its shareholder registry in an early Russian shareholder rights scandal.

Vishnyevsky was appointed two weeks ago to replace Igor Kolpakov, who resigned after the Interior Ministry said it was investigating allegations that Kolpakov might have mishandled funds. Kolpakov later told Reuters he had done nothing wrong and would clear his name.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov is locked in a battle against what he has called the "crime-ridden" world of Russian aluminium.

Vishnyevsky said of the latest changes at Krasnoyarsk that "I am quite sure this fighting is harmful for the aluminium sector in general. There is a programme on how to improve the situation at the smelter, but right now everyone is talking about politics and not economics."
Vishnyevsky is still president of Krazpa-Metals, a 50-50 joint venture between Krasnoyarsk and Glencore.
"Nobody can predict how this will develop," Vishnyevsky said but he said that Glencore would continue to work with the smelter.
Druzhinin said the saga was not yet over and the board could reshuffle its management, including him, yet again.
"I can tell you I won't be in this job for long and that at the board meeting they'll choose a new board, and the board will choose a new general director," he said.

Officials did not say whether the management change was connected to the purchase by Bank Rossiisky Kredit and a group of Russian and foreign investors on Monday of more than 47 percent of Krasnoyarsk shares.
KrAZ is already a shareholder in Rossiisky Kredit, one of Russia's 10 biggest banks.
